title: Memory Safeguard Allocator: headroom planning and KV eviction for continuous batching
creator: Priya Raman
description: Objective: design and implement a Memory Safeguard Allocator that provides predictable GPU headroom for continuous batching by explicitly budgeting weights, KV cache, and activations. This ticket covers policy design, simulator work, an admission & eviction implementation, and the rollout plan. Motivation: Production traces show transient KV pressure and activation spikes during long-running chat sessions and bursty traffic. Current behavior occasionally triggers OOM-driven hard failures or over-conservative admission throttles that reduce throughput. We need a middle ground: accurate headroom accounting + graceful, observable degradation (soft-eviction and fallback) that preserves SLA while improving utilization.
acceptance_criteria: Simulator validates that configured headroom reserves (default 6%) prevent >99.9% of measured OOMs on historical 30-day trace while delivering >=+8% throughput vs current conservative allocator
Controller exposes three configurable knobs: global headroom %, per-model KV soft-eviction threshold, and activation admission cap; changes are take-effect without node restart
KV soft-eviction implemented with per-KV TTL priority and can be toggled per-model; eviction events are logged with reason and estimated token-cost delta
Metrics added: headroom_used_ratio, kv_eviction_rate, speculative_activation_offload_count; Grafana dashboard and alert on headroom_used_ratio > 0.92
E2E rollout performed to 10% of Dedicated pools with canary policies, no increase in user-facing error-rate (target <0.1%)
design_notes: Budget model: maintain three budget buckets per serving instance - weights (resident static), KV cache (soft-evictable), activations (ephemeral). We compute GPU-resident budget = total_gpu_mem - reserved_system_overhead.

Headroom accounting: allocate a dynamic headroom reserve derived from tail-latency risk profiles per model and recent allocation churn. Default policy starts at 6% of usable GPU memory and decays/increases based on the 95th percentile of activation peaks over the last 1h.

Admission control: continuous-batching controller estimates activation footprint for incoming request using model metadata + token budget; if forecasted footprint + current_used > usable_budget - headroom, either (a) accept with activation offload to host memory for low-priority requests, (b) reduce batch or (c) soft-evict least-recently-used KV segments to free space.

KV soft-eviction policy: segment KV by conversation prefix length and recency; evict lowest-priority segments first and track token re-hydration cost. Allow configurable per-model eviction aggressiveness.

Activation offload: use pinned host pages for lower-priority request pipelines; only when offload latency < 4x GPU token latency to keep tail SLOs reasonable. Offload decision is per-request type (interactive vs background).

Trade-offs: aggressive soft-eviction raises token recompute cost and increases model latency on cache misses. Activation offload reduces memory pressure but can increase tail latencies; both are surfaced via metrics and can be disabled per-customer tier.
simulation_results: We ran a Monte Carlo replay on a representative 72h trace (multi-tenant workload) with three allocator variants: baseline (conservative fixed reserve), dynamic-headroom (this design), dynamic+aggressive-evict. Dynamic-headroom reduced average reserved idle memory by 9%, increased throughput by ~8%, and reduced OOM events to zero in replay. Aggressive-evict improved throughput further but increased 95th latency by ~12% on cache-miss-heavy sessions. Full simulation artifacts and raw logs: https://internal.redwood.ai/sims/ENG-30945/2026-03-12

testing_plan: Unit tests for budget arithmetic and edge cases (reserve exactly equals available memory).
Integration tests that inject synthetic large activations and assert admission responses and metric emissions.
Load tests on staging dedicated cluster: 24h replay with 2x peak QPS to validate headroom stability and backoff behavior.
Chaos tests: simulate node GC/driver delays and ensure allocator falls back to safe admission (reject vs offload) without data corruption.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Soft-eviction increases compute on cache-miss spikes leading to tail latency regressions. Mitigation: conservative default aggressiveness, run canary on low-SLA customers first, and add an automatic rollback if 95th-latency delta > 10%.
Risk: Offload to host memory may saturate PCIe/CPU under heavy load. Mitigation: limit offload concurrency and monitor PCIe utilization; fallback to reject when bandwidth limit reached.
Risk: Incorrect budget math could lead to under-reservation and OOM. Mitigation: multiple safety checks in controller, canary with aggressive telemetry and simulated OOM injection tests.

notes_for_reviewers: Focus review on the budget arithmetic and the assumptions in the simulation: we assume activation size per token is linear with sequence length but include a tunable multiplier for model-specific behavior.
Consider whether per-customer memory priorities should be surfaced as a numeric weight instead of tiers; that would allow finer-grained headroom allocation but requires more metadata plumbing.
Telemetry schema lives in the simulator PR; adding metrics may require a minor telemetry quota increase (ping monitoring infra).
